extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, typesetters, and publishers preparing scholarly and general publications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and rules for typography, capitalization, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation in books and similar publications (Chicago/University press house style).

rubrics_metrics.name: 46. Capitalization of scientific names (genera, orders, families)
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological matter, the scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera are capitalized, but not their English derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria (capitalized) but cotylosaurs (lowercase); Felidae but felids; Carnivora but carnivores. Also addresses capitalization of species names derived from persons or generic names and notes that in geological and medical matter species names are never capitalized (see 71).

rubrics_metrics.name: 47. Capitalize names/epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: 48. Capitalize names of solar-system bodies (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize the names of the bodies of our solar system, except 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', and 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: 49. Capitalization of institutional divisions, officers, and courses (official usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University (or institution) in official work regarding administration or curricula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the University, the School of Education (but 'the division'); the Department of Anthropology (but 'the department'); the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board); the President, the Registrar, Professor of Physics, Fellow, Scholar; Van Husen Scholarship (but 'the scholarship'); courses in Political Economy, Autumn Quarter (but 'a quarter').

rubrics_metrics.name: 50. Use capitals and small capitals for date lines, salutations, and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Set town and state in the date line, salutatory phrase at beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters or articles in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and formatting: CHICAGO, ILL., January 1, 1911 (set to the right with one em indent and preferably in smaller type). Salutation 'MY DEAR MR. SMITH:' set flush followed by a colon. Signature lines set to the right with one em indent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 51. Use of initial caps/words in resolutions, notes, and constitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words in formal documents are set in capitals: 'WHEREAS' in resolutions; 'NOTE.' in notes (followed by a period and dash); 'SECTION' introducing paragraphs in constitutions, by-laws, etc., followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice: abbreviate 'SECTION' after its first full use (e.g., 'SECTION 1. ...' then 'SEC. 2. ...'). Example formatting: NOTE. — It should be noticed that..., SECTION 1. This association shall be styled....

rubrics_metrics.name: 52. Set A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D. in small capitals and without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: A.M. and P.M. (ante/post meridiem) and B.C. and A.D. should be set in small capitals with no space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C.; 1906 A.D. (see also cross-references 22, 103, 106, 219).

rubrics_metrics.name: 53. Lowercase common words derived from proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for words of common usage that were originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally for verbs derived from proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china (lowercase), morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: 54. Lowercase minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, minor subdivisions (and their abbreviations) such as chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note should use lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n. (See cross-references: 37, no, and 237).

rubrics_metrics.name: 55. Use small initial letters for units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Units of measurement are set with small initial letters in abbreviated form when used as abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard, ft. = foot, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 56. Italic side-heads: capitalize only first word and proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads (headings in italic), capitalize only the first word and any proper names; other words are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references 172 and 280 for extended guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 57. Lowercase first word of a quotation when grammatically connected
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is immediately connected with the preceding text (e.g., by conjunction) and does not start a new sentence in the running sense, the first word of the quotation is lowercased even if the original begins a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: 58. Italicize words/phrases for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics to lend emphasis or indicate importance to words or phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case.'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 59. Italicize foreign words and short foreign passages (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text (not incorporated into English) should be italicized; likewise brief foreign sentences that are not long enough to be set in reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'Napoleon's coup d'etat'; 'De gustibus non est disputandum.' Exceptions: do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or foreign institutions/places whose English usage would require roman type (e.g., Pere Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau, the German Reichstag, the Champs Elysees), nor words sufficiently anglicized (e.g., ennui, personnel, cafe, naive).

rubrics_metrics.name: 60. Italicize titles of publications (books, pamphlets, periodicals) but use roman for biblical books and ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of books, plays, essays, long poems, pamphlets, treatises, tractates, documents, and periodicals should be set in italics; in bibliographies or long lists this may be departed from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Chicago Tribune, the New York Times. Note: books of the Bible and ancient manuscripts are set in roman. Botanical Gazette exception: it uses italics for titles in text only; in footnotes, roman; its own name printed in caps and small caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: 61. Italicize certain Latin/legal reference abbreviations; do not italicize common abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize reference abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc., circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize: cf., e.g., i.e., v. (versus), viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 62. Use italics for cross-reference words in indexes and errata lists
rubrics_metrics.description: In an index or similar compilation, set 'See' and 'See also' in italics to differentiate them from the context; in errata lists set 'for' and 'read' in italics to separate incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee.

rubrics_metrics.name: 63. Italicize names of parties and certain legal prefixes in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: In citations of legal causes, italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant and the titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, In the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: 64. Formatting address lines in speeches, reports, and letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush on a separate line with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:' ; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.'; 'DEAR SIR: I take pleasure in announcing ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: 65. Formatting signatures with titles and positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for placing a position or title after a signature: if one word, run into same line; if more than one but not longer than the name, center first letter under the name line and indent one em on right; if longer than the name, center the name over the second line and set the title flush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ARTHUR P. MAGUIRE, Secretary; CARTER H. HARRISON, Mayor of Chicago; CHARLES M. GAYLEY, Professor of English Language and Literature. Rules subject to special-case exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: 66. Use of a), b), c) and a, b, c for subdivisions and fractional verse/page annotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c) to mark subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if 'run in'); use a, b, c affixed to numbers of verse, page, etc., to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:3a (notation of fractional part).

rubrics_metrics.name: 67. Use letters to designate unknown quantities and lines in mathematical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, and similar elements in algebraic, geometrical, and related matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac + bc = c(a + b); the lines ad and AD; the n-th power.

rubrics_metrics.name: 68. Use letters in legends and cross-references to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters in legends or text that refer to corresponding letters in illustrations should be used and set as letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: 69. References to particular letters (names of letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters themselves, use phrasing like 'the letter u, a small v.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concerns typographic references to letters as objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: 70. Use s. and d. after numerals for shillings and pence
rubrics_metrics.description: When listing pre-decimal British currency following numerals, use 's.' and 'd.' for shillings and pence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 35s. 6d. (See also 270).

rubrics_metrics.name: 71. Italicization and formatting of scientific names and astronomical designations
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, generic and species names used together have the generic name in nominative singular and are italicized; in medical matter, such names are generally printed in roman. For astronomical/astrophysical names: (a) Greek/Latin/Arabic names of planets, satellites, constellations, and individual stars; (b) designations from well-known catalogs (Messier, NGC, Flamsteed); (c) chemical element symbols; (d) Fraunhofer lower-case letters are italicized, but Fraunhofer capital letters and spectral type letters are not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri. Astronomy examples: Jupiter, Tethys, Lyra, Antares, λ Orionis; M 13; N.G.C. 6165; 85 Pegasi. Chemical symbols: H, Ca, Ti (not italicized). Fraunhofer letters: a, b, g, h (italicized); A–H and K (not italicized); spectral types As, B3, M b (not italicized). See also rules 46, 48, 123.

rubrics_metrics.name: 72. Italicize the word 'Resolved.' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions, set the word 'Resolved.' (formatting consistent with rule on use of italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference: see also rule 39.

rubrics_metrics.name: 73. Use of 'Continued' after headlines or 'To be continued' at ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, the word 'Continued' is usually used; at the end of articles use 'To be continued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued; end-of-article note: [To be continued]. See also 179.

rubrics_metrics.name: 74. Put citations run into text between quotation marks and in roman
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations (passages from an author quoted in his own words and run into the text) should be enclosed in quotation marks and printed in roman type (i.e., 'roman-quote').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 85 for long quotations set in smaller type.

rubrics_metrics.name: 75. Use quotation marks for successive quotations from different authors or works without intervening original matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors or different works by the same author that follow each other, uninterrupted by intervening original matter or references to sources, should be enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rules 85–87 on reduced citations and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 76. Put a word or phrase accompanied by its definition in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word or phrase is immediately given with its definition, the word or phrase should be in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: 77. Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, or ironical words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Place unusual, technical, or ironical words or phrases in quotation marks to direct attention to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; 'so-called' man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 78. Use quotation marks for English equivalents in translations
rubrics_metrics.description: In translations, place the English equivalent of a foreign word, phrase, or passage in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: 79. Use quotation marks for words/phrases to which attention is directed
rubrics_metrics.description: When calling attention to a particular term or phrase in the text, enclose it in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 80. Put serial titles in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of series or serial titles should be enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 81. Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of shorter poems should be set in quotation marks (contrast with rule 60 for longer poems/books).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 82. Use quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions and shorter works
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters) and titles of papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc., should be in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; articles 'Cross', 'Crucifixion' in Hastings' Dictionary of the Bible; note: Botanical Gazette in footnotes does not use quotation marks for such titles. References to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index of a specific work should be set with capitals without quotation marks: Preface, p. iii.

rubrics_metrics.name: 83. Use quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Ship names are placed in quotation marks, often accompanied by official prefixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 84. Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of pictures and works of art should be enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 85. Set long prose and poetry quotations in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose extracts that would make five or more lines in the smaller type and poetry citations of two lines or more should be set in reduced (smaller) type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated prose quotation may be run into the text if organically related to the argument. A short quotation of one or two lines closely adjacent to longer reduced extracts may also be set reduced for uniform appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 86. Rules for reducing point size for citations
rubrics_metrics.description: When reducing quotations, follow specified reductions of point sizes (e.g., from n-pt and 12-pt to 10-pt, from 9-pt to 8-pt, from 8-pt to 6-pt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule cross-reference 252 for detailed typographic reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 87. Reduced citations generally omit quotation marks and avoid combining with italics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced (smaller-type) citations should not have quotation marks except in special cases described elsewhere; similarly, quotation marks should not usually be used in connection with italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions noted in rule 75 and related entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 88. Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when they indicate omitted material
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when those indicate that part of the quoted matter is omitted — clarity in each case is the guiding criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text show inclusion and exclusion based on whether 'etc.' stands for omitted part of the quoted material or is commentary outside the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 89. Repeat opening quotation marks for each paragraph of a broken quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose set with quotation marks is broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the indication that the material is a continuous quotation across paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: 90. 'Clear' quotation marks when alignment is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: If alignment of quoted lines is desired, set the quotation marks so they project beyond the line of alignment (i.e., 'cleared').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example shows quotation marks set to align visually with block formatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: 91. Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and alternate with single for nested quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation, use single quotes; alternate back to double for a third level and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that "the words, 'freedom' and 'liberty,' ..."' '

rubrics_metrics.name: 92. Spell out civil and military titles preceding the name (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: All civil and military titles and forms of address preceding a name should be spelled out except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; abbreviate Esq. following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not, except in quotations, use 'the Rev.' or 'the Hon.'; treat exceptions and context accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: 93. Spell out Christian (given) names and 'von' as part of the name
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian (given) names such as George, Charles, John should be spelled out (not Geo., Chas., Jno.), except where abbreviated forms are used in quoted matter or original signatures; treat 'von' as part of a person's name and spell it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 240 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 94. Spell out numbers under three digits in ordinary reading matter (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out all numbers of less than three digits unless they are statistical/technical or occur in long groups; treat exceptions such as decimals, degrees, money, percentages as figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' vs. 'He spent 128 days in the hospital.' Use figures for 10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, $1,000, etc. Treat groups consistently (if the largest contains three or more digits, use figures for all).

rubrics_metrics.name: 95. Spell out round numbers (approximate figures) but use numerals for specific figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Round/approximate numbers (e.g., five hundred) are spelled out; specific figures like 550 are written in numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but write '550' if precise). For numbers like 1,500 spelled out for special reasons, write 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 96. Spell out numbers that begin sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, regardless of size, that commence a sentence should be spelled out in ordinary reading matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children...' If impracticable, reconstruct the sentence to avoid starting with a numeral.

rubrics_metrics.name: 97. Spell out isolated sums of money in ordinary reading matter
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sum of money occurs in isolation in ordinary reading matter, spell it out; when multiple monetary figures occur close together or in statistical contexts, use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The admission was two dollars.' vs. 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 98. Spell out time of day in ordinary reading; use figures for statistical/enumerative contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary prose, write times in words (e.g., at four; at half-past two); in statistical contexts, enumerations, or when using A.M./P.M., use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example statistical usage: at 4:15 P.M. (omit 'o'clock' in such connections).

rubrics_metrics.name: 99. Spell out ages in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words in ordinary prose (e.g., 'eighty years and four months old').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'children between six and fourteen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 100. Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, military/political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words for numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, and similar formal enumerations unless brevity requires otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifteenth Infantry N.G.; Fifth Avenue. See rules 7, 8, and 13 for context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101. References to particular decades use phrase form
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to particular decades using phrases (e.g., 'in the nineties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid numeral-only shorthand in ordinary prose unless context demands it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102. Spell out names of months except in statistical/long enumerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months are spelled out in ordinary prose, except in statistical contexts or long enumerations where brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from January 1 to April 15 (omit ordinal suffixes like st, d, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: 103. Use 'United States' spelled out in most contexts (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'United States' out except in quotations and certain abbreviated contexts such as 'General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'; in footnotes and similar references: U.S. Geological Survey.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references: see rules 22, 52, 106.

rubrics_metrics.name: 104. Spell out 'Railroad (-way)', 'Fort', 'Mount', 'Port' in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: In geographical appellations, spell out terms like Railroad (-way), Fort, Mount, and Port rather than abbreviating in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not 'R.R.' or 'Ry.'); Fort Wayne; Port Huron; Mount Elias.

rubrics_metrics.name: 105. General guidance: spell out names of publications in most cases, with flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally spell out names of publications; modification may be needed in particular instances — consider expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference. When in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that good taste more readily condones minor offenses in this direction than the reverse; exceptions exist for special contexts (e.g., bibliographies).

rubrics_metrics.name: 106. Abbreviate names of U.S. states/territories following town names using set abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a state, territory, or possession name follows a town, use the prescribed abbreviations without spaces between abbreviation letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ala., La., Ore., Ala., Alaska, Me., Pa., Ariz., Mass., P.I. = Philippine Islands, P.R. = Porto Rico, etc. See cross-references to rules 22, 52, 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: 107. Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand in technical bibliographic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matters such as footnote references and bibliographies, abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' for 'and' in firm names; in ordinary text, 'Company' and 'Brothers' may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; in text: 'Harper Brothers have recently published ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: 108. Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' with usage preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' before names of places (St. Louis, St. Peter's Church, SS. Peter and Paul). Preferably omit 'St.' in references to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Luke, Paul, Augustine (not 'St. Luke', 'St. Paul', etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 109. Abbreviations for books of the Bible and common versions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standardized abbreviations for books of the Old and New Testaments, Apocrypha, and for commonly cited Bible versions (A.V., R.V., A.R.V., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive list provided (e.g., Gen., Exod., Ps., Matt., Mark, Luke, John, etc.) and versions: A.V. = Authorized Version, R.V. = Revised Version, LXX = Septuagint, Vulg. = Vulgate, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: 110. (bibliographic abbreviations) Abbreviate terms like Vol., No., Ps., chap., p., pp., Fig.
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical material, abbreviate volume, number, psalm, division, chapter, article, section, page, column, verse, line, note, figure, etc., when followed by numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I (Vols.), No. 1 (Nos.), Ps. 20 (Pss.), chap. ii (chaps.), art. iii (arts.), sec. 4 (secs.), p. 5 (pp.), col. 6 (cols.), vs. 7 (vss.), l. 8 (ll.), n. 9 (nn.), Fig. 7 (Figs.); pp. 5–7; pp. 5ff.

rubrics_metrics.name: 111. Metric and common measurement symbols after numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations and symbols of the metric system and common measures following numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; c.m. = cubic meter, gm. = gram, gr. = grain, h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second, lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; A.U. = Angstrom Units, H.P. = horse-power, C. = centigrade, F. = Fahrenheit, L.C.M. = lowest common multiple.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112. In extracts follow office style for modern authors; preserve originals when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: For extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ only slightly, apply office (house) style; for Old English or where faithfulness is essential, follow the original. Titles must be accurately quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgement to preserve authorial features when required by the context or writer's plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: 113. Form possessives of proper names ending in s or sibilants by syllabic rule
rubrics_metrics.description: For proper names ending in 's' or another sibilant: if monosyllabic, form possessive by adding apostrophe + s; if more than one syllable, form possessive with apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions; 'for convenience' sake.'

rubrics_metrics.name: 114. Use 'a' before sounded h, long u, and the word 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before words beginning with sounded h, long u, and before 'one' use the indefinite article 'a' (not 'an').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic, a historical, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: 115. Use or separate ligature 'ae'/'oe' in Latin quotations vs modern languages
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the ligature 'ae' and 'oe' (render as separate letters) in quotations from Latin and anglicized derivatives from Latin or Greek via Latin where 'e' has not been substituted; retain ligature in quotations from Old English and modern languages where correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In Latin quotations separate letters in 'Aurea prima sata est...' but retain ligature in 'Euvres de Balzac, chef-d'oeuvre' and similar contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 116. Differentiate 'farther' and 'further' by distinct senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to mean 'more remote' or physical distance; use 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: 117. Use 'O' (vocative) without a comma; 'Oh' (exclamation) with a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: In forms of address (vocative) use 'O' without a following comma; for exclamations use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?' (See rule 40.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 118. Retain or omit final -e in participles according to termination patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles ending with a syllable beginning with a vowel retain the final 'e' in the primary word (e.g., agreeing, dyeing, eyeing), while others omit the 'e' (e.g., acknowledging, gluing, judging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of examples illustrate which participles retain or omit final 'e'; follow examples as pattern guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 119. Preferred spellings for a long list of words (American usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide the house-preferred spellings for numerous commonly variant words (e.g., abridgment, center, favor, aluminum, behavior, color, theater, traveler, etc.) and instruct to make certain compounds one word (anyone, someone, everyone, today, tomorrow, tonight, cannot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive list given; note many Americanized forms (center not centre; color not colour; theater not theatre) and other specific preferences. Also distinguish sometimes vs some time(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: 120. Use -ise vs -ize terminations according to specified lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate words that should be spelled with -ise endings from those with -ize (-yze) endings; extensive lists for each termination are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (selective): -ise: advertise, comprise, advise, exercise, revise; -ize: aggrandize, analyze, civilize, energize, organize, realize, summarize, utilize. Full lists in the rule give mapping for many verbs/nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: 121. Punctuation marks match the font/style of the preceding character
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai!' the regiment stormed the hill; Luke 4:16a; No. 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: 122. Use a period to mark the end of a complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: A period indicates the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 125 for further punctuation context.

rubrics_metrics.name: 123. Put a period after abbreviations (with specified exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a period after all abbreviations except where mechanical necessity compels omission (e.g., when letters omitted in the middle of a word are shown by an apostrophe), and treat metric symbols as abbreviations (period used), but do not use periods for chemical symbols, the phrase 'per cent', or book format abbreviations like 4to/8vo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas. (see 93), ibid., s.v.; 10 mm.; but: m'f'g pl't (= manufacturing plant), O, Fe; 2 per cent (see 94); 4to, 8vo.
